INTRODUCTION Little palaeomagnetic work has been done on Palaeozoic rocks in Tasmania. The only published palaeomagnetic study of the Tasmanian Ordovician is by Briden (1967), who found that,the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of certain Lower Ordovician sandstones represented a secondary magnetization. Briden regarded this as resulting from regional heating during the Tertiary. The limestones in the Ida Bay region of southern Tasmania are amongst the least folded and the least altered Ordovician rocks in Tasmania. It was hoped, therefore, that they would retain a primary magnetization, thus allowing the determination of the palaeolatitude of _Tasmania at the time of limestone deposition. This study was initially undertaken by one of the authors (C.S.) as part of a broader sedimentological study of Ordovician rocks in the Ida Bay area. The laboratory work in this project was undertaken at the palaeomagnetic laboratory of the Australian National University in Canberra. GEOLOGICAL SETTING The limestones studied here belong to the Ordovician Gordon Subgroup (Corbett and Banks 1974) and outcrop on Marble Hill (146° 51'E. 43° 28 1 S) near the township of Ida Bay in southern Tasmania (fig. 1). Oriented core samples of 2.5 cm diameter and 3 to 10 cm length were collected with a portable, gasoline-powered drill. In the laboratory, the cores were cut to 2.3 cm length and stored in a magnetically shielded room ( about 100 gammas residual field) in order to eliminate possible viscous magnetization. The samples remained in this room throughout the experimental procedures. A cryogenic magnetometer, interfaced with a computer, was used for the measurements. All samples were sub­ jected to thermal demagnetization in an ambient field of less than 3 gammas. The carbonate rocks were heated to 200, 250, 300, 350, and 400°C, and the elastic rocks to 200, 250, 400, 500, and 600°c. RESULTS The natural remanent magnetization of most carbonate samples (Grupera and Paso Hondo Formations) had a strong component aligned with the present geomagnetic field (Fig. 3). After heating to 250°C, a reversed magnetization was generally ob­ tained, and demagnetization to 300°c and 350°c simply improved the clustering. ABSTRACT The paleomagnetic analysis of samples from the lower Permian Paso Hondo y Grupera Forma­ tions, collected near Chicomuselo, Chiapas, yields an equatorial latitude and implies that the sampling area was in a position rotated 22° counterclockwise relative to cratonic North Amer­ ica. By contrast, the poleposition obtained from the Pennsylvanian-Permian Yododeiie Forma­ tion, collected near Nochixtlan, Oaxaca, closely agrees with equivalent North American data. This implies that the Isthmus of Tchuantepec represents a major discontinuity. The new results support our previous suggestion that Mcsoamerica consisted of a series of tectonic blocks. • lnstitute for Geophysics and De

The sites were chosen from aerial photographic maps and from geological maps kindly made available to us by Mooser. LABORATORY PROCEDURES Samples were obtained with a hand corer. They were oriented by means of a mag­ netic inclinometer and in some cases additionally with a sun-compass. From each site 2 or 3 pilot-specimens were demagnetized in an increasing alternating field to get the range of field strengths, at which the palaeomagnetic directions were most stable. This range was determined using Zijdetveld diagrams and a stability index according to Symons and Stupavsky ( 1974). The other specimens were demagne­ tized in alternating fields within this stable range. A Digico spinner magnetometer was used to determine the magnetization. Demagnetization was carried out with a Schonstedt af-demagnetizer and, above 80 kA/m ( 1000 Oe ), with a tumbler appa­ ratus. Some samples were thermally demagnetized using a Schonstedt apparatus; their mag11etization was measured with a Czechoslovakian JR-3 spinner magneto­ meter. section_candidates.excerpt: RESUMEN Resultados paleomagneticos de aproximadamente 500 muestras orientadas colectadas en 59 si­ tios de la seccion este del eje volcanico trans-Mexicano se presentan en este trabajo. Las rocas {gneas estudiadas son del Plioceno y Cuaternario, con la excepcion del macizo de Palma Sola, de edad Mioceno. Los resultados paleomagneticos se usan para correlacionar con resultados geoqu{micos y geologicos del area y con resultados paleomagneticos de Norteamerica y Mexico. Los resultados no indican movimiento relativo signiflcante entre Norteamerica y la seccion cen­ tral-este de Mexico en el periodo estudiado. ABSTRACT About 500 oriented samples were taken from 59 sites in the eastern part of the Trans Mexican Volcanic Belt. The investigated igneous rocks are of Pliocene to Quaternary, and additionally in the Palma Sola Massif of Miocene age. Besides correlations with geochemical and geological results it was the intention to determine the mean poles from the palaeomagnetic directions for the Quaternary and upper Tertiary. Serdan, Jalapa and Palma Sola (N of Veracruz), belonging to the eas­ tern part of the Trans Mexican Volcanic Belt (TMVB) (Fig. 1). The work included aerial-photography interpretation, mapping and sampling for geochemical investiga­ tions and radiometric datings. Also in 1980; about 500 oriented samples were taken for palaeomagnetic work. Besides special investigations in conjunction with the geochemical and geological investigations it was the aim of those measurements to obtain new data for the secular variation of the earth's magnetic field at this lati­ tude, as well as to search for possible tectonic motions between the sampling area and North America. The plate tectonic evolution of Mexico is still unknown because only 3: few re­ liable palaeomagnetic data are available today. agnetic data are available today. Starting from reconstructions of the continental drift as e.g. the well known "Bullard-fit", Mexico obviously could not have been part of the North American plate in former times, as this would imply large overlapping with South America. Therefore, several models were proposed which allow Mexico to arrive at the today position by movements along different postulated shear zones (e.g. Dickinson and Coney, 1980; Gose et al., 1980). Most authors assume that the main movement occurred soon after the opening of the Atlantic. Other researchers assume movements until Tertiary times (e.g. Walper, 1980). Some palaeomagnetic results seem to support this idea (Urrutia-Fucugauchi and Pal, 1977; Urrutia-Fucugauchi, 1981 b) as well as the concept of microplate ro­ tations near the TMVB (Urrutia-Fucugauchi, 1981a). Samples were, therefore, taken from the eastern part of the TMVB, dating back to the upper Tertiary, to examine if such movements could be detected in this region. section_candidates.excerpt: RESUMEN Resultados paleomagneticos de aproximadamente 500 muestras orientadas colectadas en 59 si­ tios de la seccion este del eje volcanico trans-Mexicano se presentan en este trabajo. Las rocas {gneas estudiadas son del Plioceno y Cuaternario, con la excepcion del macizo de Palma Sola, de edad Mioceno. Los resultados paleomagneticos se usan para correlacionar con resultados geoqu{micos y geologicos del area y con resultados paleomagneticos de Norteamerica y Mexico. Los resultados no indican movimiento relativo signiflcante entre Norteamerica y la seccion cen­ tral-este de Mexico en el periodo estudiado. ABSTRACT About 500 oriented samples were taken from 59 sites in the eastern part of the Trans Mexican Volcanic Belt. The investigated igneous rocks are of Pliocene to Quaternary, and additionally in the Palma Sola Massif of Miocene age. Besides correlations with geochemical and geological results it was the intention to determine the mean poles from the palaeomagnetic directions for the Quaternary and upper Tertiary. The results indicate no significant relative motion between North America and eastern Mexico during this time. * Jnstitut fur Geophysik, Universitiit Munster Gievenhecker Weg 61, D-4400 Miinster, Germany. ** Abteilung Geologie der l'achgruppe Geographic,

Serdan, Jalapa and Palma Sola (N of Veracruz), belonging to the eas­ tern part of the Trans Mexican Volcanic Belt (TMVB) (Fig. 1). The work included aerial-photography interpretation, mapping and sampling for geochemical investiga­ tions and radiometric datings. Also in 1980; about 500 oriented samples were taken for palaeomagnetic work. Besides special investigations in conjunction with the geochemical and geological investigations it was the aim of those measurements to obtain new data for the secular variation of the earth's magnetic field at this lati­ tude, as well as to search for possible tectonic motions between the sampling area and North America. The plate tectonic evolution of Mexico is still unknown because only 3: few re­ liable palaeomagnetic data are available today. agnetic data are available today. Starting from reconstructions of the continental drift as e.g. the well known "Bullard-fit", Mexico obviously could not have been part of the North American plate in former times, as this would imply large overlapping with South America. Therefore, several models were proposed which allow Mexico to arrive at the today position by movements along different postulated shear zones (e.g. Dickinson and Coney, 1980; Gose et al., 1980). Most authors assume that the main movement occurred soon after the opening of the Atlantic. Other researchers assume movements until Tertiary times (e.g. Walper, 1980). Some palaeomagnetic results seem to support this idea (Urrutia-Fucugauchi and Pal, 1977; Urrutia-Fucugauchi, 1981 b) as well as the concept of microplate ro­ tations near the TMVB (Urrutia-Fucugauchi, 1981a). Samples were, therefore, taken from the eastern part of the TMVB, dating back to the upper Tertiary, to examine if such movements could be detected in this region. OUTLINE OF GEOLOGY, COLLECTING OF ORIENTED SAMPLES Oriented samples of Upper Carboniferous (Stephanian), Permian and Triassic sediments were collected from NW Bulgaria for palaeomagnetic analyses. Studies were concentrated especial- ly on "red beds" dominated by sandstones, claystones and quartzites. The investigated rocks showed an essential difference in petrographical, mineralogical and chemical compositions, as well as in their tecture and structure, all resulting from different palaeotectonic, palaeogeographic, facies and palaeoclimatic development history [1, 2]. Upper Palaeozoic rocks were deposited under various palaeogeographic conditions. An ancient mountain system of the Variscides trending NW--SE was formed in the western part of Bulgaria. Sediments of Stephanian age were laid down in intra-orogenic depressions; diluvial, stream, lacustrine and mud sediments were thus formed. Most depressions developed in grabens bounded by tectonic lines which were activated during the early Permian.

Laboratory criteria were found which permitted to distinguish samples suitable for palaeomagnetic analyses from those representing rocks totally or almost totally chemically reworked during their history. Palaeomagnetic directions and pole positions derived from Stephanian, Lower Permian and Triassic rocks from the southern margin of the Moesian Platform are compatible with the values obtained for the tectonically stable North- European Platform. OUTLINE OF GEOLOGY, COLLECTING OF ORIENTED SAMPLES Oriented samples of Upper Carboniferous (Stephanian), Permian and Triassic sediments were collected from NW Bulgaria for palaeomagnetic analyses. Studies were concentrated especial- ly on "red beds" dominated by sandstones, claystones and quartzites. The investigated rocks showed an essential difference in petrographical, mineralogical and chemical compositions, as well as in their tecture and structure, all resulting from different palaeotectonic, palaeogeographic, facies and palaeoclimatic development history [1, 2]. Upper Palaeozoic rocks were deposited under various palaeogeographic conditions. An ancient mountain system of the Variscides trending NW--SE was formed in the western part of Bulgaria. Sediments of Stephanian age were laid down in intra-orogenic depressions; diluvial, stream, lacustrine and mud sediments were thus formed. Most depressions developed in grabens bounded by tectonic lines which were activated during the early Permian. Lava locally ascended along these tectonic lines towards the surface. OUTLINE OF GEOLOGY, COLLECTING OF ORIENTED SAMPLES Oriented samples of Upper Carboniferous (Stephanian), Permian and Triassic sediments were collected from NW Bulgaria for palaeomagnetic analyses. Studies were concentrated especial- ly on "red beds" dominated by sandstones, claystones and quartzites. The investigated rocks showed an essential difference in petrographical, mineralogical and chemical compositions, as well as in their tecture and structure, all resulting from different palaeotectonic, palaeogeographic, facies and palaeoclimatic development history [1, 2]. Upper Palaeozoic rocks were deposited under various palaeogeographic conditions. An ancient mountain system of the Variscides trending NW--SE was formed in the western part of Bulgaria. Sediments of Stephanian age were laid down in intra-orogenic depressions; diluvial, stream, lacustrine and mud sediments were thus formed. Most depressions developed in grabens bounded by tectonic lines which were activated during the early Permian.

An ancient mountain system of the Variscides trending NW--SE was formed in the western part of Bulgaria. Sediments of Stephanian age were laid down in intra-orogenic depressions; diluvial, stream, lacustrine and mud sediments were thus formed. Most depressions developed in grabens bounded by tectonic lines which were activated during the early Permian. Lava locally ascended along these tectonic lines towards the surface. This period was succeeded by an intense peneplana- tion, at which time clastic rocks were being deposited while the climate changed from humid to arid. Thick sediments layers were accumulated in the Lower Permian (Autunian, Saxonian). In Upper Permian (Thuringian), after other tectonic movements, rocks were deposited especially in deltas. Triassic sediments developed under quite different conditions [1]. A vast depression filled with water of marine nature was formed over the entire territory of western Bulgaria. Since the Variscan mountain system was already a peneplane, equal sedimentation conditions prevailed not only in the study area but also far to the NE and SW. HATTORI and K. HIROOKA * Geological Laboratory, Fukui University, Fukui 910 (Japan) (Submitted at March 2, 1978; revised version accepted August 11, 1978) ABSTRACT Hattori, I. and Hirooka, K., 1979. Paleomagnetic results from Permian greenstones in central Japan and their geologic significance. Tectonophysics, 57 : 21 l-235. A systematic paleomagnetic study has been made of Permian greenstones and asso- ciated sediments from the inner belt of central Japan. The greenstones are generally meta- morpho

aleomagnetic study has been made of Permian greenstones and asso- ciated sediments from the inner belt of central Japan. The greenstones are generally meta- morphosed into the zeolite facies to greenschist facies grade. The intensity of the natural remanent magnetization of the greenstones decreases with increase of metamorphic grade toward the greenschist facies. Metamorphism as low or lower than the greenschist facies grade does not create chemical remanent magnetization in the greenstones. Reliable mag- netic directions were obtained from the greenstones and associated sediments occurring in the lowest grade metamorphic zones after thermal demagnetization and alternating field demagnetization. After correction of the magnetic directions with respect to the folding axes and bedding planes, the Permian magnetic inclination in Japan was deduced yielding the suggestion that Japan was situated in an equatorial region in the late Paleozoic period, perhaps as part of a missing continent, Pacifica. Since then, the Far East microplate including Japan migrated toward the north, and collided with the Asian mainland in the late Mesozoic. INTRODUCTION Many paleomagnetic studies have been made on late Mesozoic and Ceno- zoic rocks in Japan, and Yaskawa and Nakajima (1974) have summarized the avai

d in central Japan (Hattori and Hirooka, 1977). But, the data are too few to allow any conclu- sion to be drawn and systematic studies of Paleozoic paleomagnetism are necessary to delineate the drift path of Japan and to gain a better under- standing of the paleogeography relevant to Japan in Paleozoic time. The systematic paleomagnetic study described in this paper has been directed toward the lower to middle Permian greenstones of the northern part of the inner belt of central Japan (Fig. 1). The metamorphic grade in this region is generally low and the greenstones have been comparatively well preserved. The greenstones are generally meta- morphosed into the zeolite facies to greenschist facies grade. The intensity of the natural remanent magnetization of the greenstones decreases with increase of metamorphic grade toward the greenschist facies. Metamorphism as low or lower than the greenschist facies grade does not create chemical remanent magnetization in the greenstones. Reliable mag- netic directions were obtained from the greenstones and associated sediments occurring in the lowest grade metamorphic zones after thermal demagnetization and alternating field demagnetization. Paleomagnetic evidence for non-Apenninic origin of the Sila nappes (Calabria). Tectonophysics, 60: 169-188 The magnetization of Lower Permian rocks from Sila has a mean direction D = 56.5’, I = +20.4’ with ogs = 9.1’ after correction for Upper Neogene tilting. A further correc- tion for the attitude of the nappes after their Middle Miocene emplacement establishes paleolatitudes consistent with those from the Lower Permian Tethys. The remarkable internal consistency of the data has not supported the distinction of units with opposite vergences within the Sila crystalline nappes. The declination indicates that the Sila massif has rotated counter-clockwise by about 90’ relative to the Apennines, Sardinia and the Southern Alps and therefore the well-known Apenninic rotation alone does not account for the total change of direction in tectonic transport. Accordingly, the structural trends of tectonic phases older than the emplacement time of the Calabrian nappes should no longer be referred to present-day geographic coordinates. The post-Late Cretaceous motion relative to the north Calabrian Apennines enhances the geotectonic role of the northern boundary of the Calab

ues in the interpretation of the structure of the Mediterranean. The Sangineto line marks its northern boundary in Calabria and the Taor- mina line marks its southern boundary in Sicily; both lines have been assumed by diverging modern interpretations to represent the Africa- Europe boundary. THE TECTONIC SETTING The allochthonous character of all the exposed pre-Miocene rocks piled up in complex nappes is now generally accepted. The occurrence among them 170 of nappes with Hercynian plutonites and metamorphic rocks (Calabride units by Ogniben, 1969) has fostered divergent speculations on the original loca- tion, the history of deformation, and the transport of the fragmented con- tinental crust. In recent interpretations some models consider all structures as originally belonging to an Apenninic domain or geo-syncline with most, but not all, directions of transport from the west (e.g. Ogniben, 1969). Dubois, 1976 and other authors assume that a north-African chain was fragmented, deformed and displaced by the Europe-Africa collision. Micro- plate models advocate the drifting of the entire crust of Calabria from a frag- mented Alpine belt east of Sardinia, in spite of the known allochthony of all exposed terreins and of the lack of information on the nature of the bas

tion, the history of deformation, and the transport of the fragmented con- tinental crust. In recent interpretations some models consider all structures as originally belonging to an Apenninic domain or geo-syncline with most, but not all, directions of transport from the west (e.g. Ogniben, 1969). Dubois, 1976 and other authors assume that a north-African chain was fragmented, deformed and displaced by the Europe-Africa collision. Micro- plate models advocate the drifting of the entire crust of Calabria from a frag- mented Alpine belt east of Sardinia, in spite of the known allochthony of all exposed terreins and of the lack of information on the nature of the base- ment (Alvarez et al., 1974). When units from an Alpine chain are considered as the source of the upper nappes with Hercynian rocks, such as the Sila nappes, coming to override the structures of the Apenninic chain, different phases of directions of transport are required. According to Haccard et al. (1972): there was first an Alp-Apennine compression, then tectonic transport from the east, and subsequently Apen- ninic transport from the west, the southwest and the south. According to Mascle and Grandjacquet (1978), Cretaceous transport from the south or southeast and east was followed by Upper Cretaceous

erms of present geography; in the second case, directions are chosen according to the requirements of the pro- posed models. The complexities of the interpretations stem from an extrem- ely intricate geologic history. Amodio Morelli et al. (1976) have made an interpretative review of models put forward to explain the origin of the Calabrian-Peloritan arc. In this reconstruction the Alpine nappes with vergence toward Europe overrode Apenninic terrain with southeasterly and easterly vergence toward the African foreland during the Miocene. The upper nappes with Hercynian ter- rains from the Sila massif are split into two units with opposite vergences: a lower Longobucco-Longi-Taormina nappe with African vergence and an overlying “incertae sedis” Mt. Gariglione unit (Fig. 1). Both units are made up of plutonites (granodiorites, tonalites, porphyritic and aplitic dykes) with associated high and medium-grade metamorphites (migmatites, amphibolites, gneisses, gabbroids). Palaeomagnetism and deforma- tion of the Mesozoic continental margin in Sicily. Tectonophysics, 61: 391-407. The pre-erogenic morphology of the west Sicilian Mesozoic continental margin was characterised by platforms and basins elongated more or less parallel to the ancient june- tion between ocean and continent. The deformation of this continental margin during the Miocene gave rise to a number of thrust sheets which were transported southwards where they rest against the stable Iblean plateau. Bight thrust sheets have been sampled for palaeomagnetism in order to establish the amount of rotation, relative to Iblei, which occurred during emplacement. Cfockwise rotations of large magnitude appear to have taken place, and these rotations are considered to be refated to the emplacement of the Calabrian-Peloritani structure onto this continental margin. INTRODUCTION The geological structure of western Sicily is formed by a number of piled thrust sheets. The vergence of these imbricated units is to the south where they rest against the stable Iblean plateau (Fig. 1). The amount of tectonic transportation increases towards the north of the island where the tectonic units occupying the top of the thrust pile are cropping out. Palaeomagnetism and deforma- tion of the Mesozoic continental margin in Sicily. Tectonophysics, 61: 391-407. The pre-erogenic morphology of the west Sicilian Mesozoic continental margin was characterised by platforms and basins elongated more or less parallel to the ancient june- tion between ocean and continent. The deformation of this continental margin during the Miocene gave rise to a number of thrust sheets which were transported southwards where they rest against the stable Iblean plateau. Bight thrust sheets have been sampled for palaeomagnetism in order to establish the amount of rotation, relative to Iblei, which occurred during emplacement. Cfockwise rotations of large magnitude appear to have taken place, and these rotations are considered to be refated to the emplacement of the Calabrian-Peloritani structure onto this continental margin. INTRODUCTION The geological structure of western Sicily is formed by a number of piled thrust sheets. The vergence of these imbricated units is to the south where they rest against the stable Iblean plateau (Fig. 1). The pre-erogenic morphology of the west Sicilian Mesozoic continental margin was characterised by platforms and basins elongated more or less parallel to the ancient june- tion between ocean and continent. The deformation of this continental margin during the Miocene gave rise to a number of thrust sheets which were transported southwards where they rest against the stable Iblean plateau. INTRODUCTION The geological structure of western Sicily is formed by a number of piled thrust sheets. The vergence of these imbricated units is to the south where they rest against the stable Iblean plateau (Fig. 1). Palaeomagnetism and deforma- tion of the Mesozoic continental margin in Sicily. Tectonophysics, 61: 391-407. The pre-erogenic morphology of the west Sicilian Mesozoic continental margin was characterised by platforms and basins elongated more or less parallel to the ancient june- tion between ocean and continent. The deformation of this continental margin during the Miocene gave rise to a number of thrust sheets which were transported southwards where they rest against the stable Iblean plateau. Bight thrust sheets have been sampled for palaeomagnetism in order to establish the amount of rotation, relative to Iblei, which occurred during emplacement. Cfockwise rotations of large magnitude appear to have taken place, and these rotations are considered to be refated to the emplacement of the Calabrian-Peloritani structure onto this continental margin. INTRODUCTION The geological structure of western Sicily is formed by a number of piled thrust sheets. The vergence of these imbricated units is to the south where they rest against the stable Iblean plateau (Fig. 1). The amount of tectonic transportation increases towards the north of the island where the tectonic units occupying the top of the thrust pile are cropping out. The timing of progressive deformation from north to south can be established stra~~aphi- tally because sedimentation was more or less continuous during the Neogene tectonic transport of the thrust sheets. A number of structural-stratigraphic units may be defined (Figs. 2 and 3). These units are geological bodies which display homogeneity in facies and tectonic behaviour, and are derived from pre-existing palaeogeographic units. Palaeomagnetism and deforma- tion of the Mesozoic continental margin in Sicily. Tectonophysics, 61: 391-407. The pre-erogenic morphology of the west Sicilian Mesozoic continental margin was characterised by platforms and basins elongated more or less parallel to the ancient june- tion between ocean and continent. The deformation of this continental margin during the Miocene gave rise to a number of thrust sheets which were transported southwards where they rest against the stable Iblean plateau. Bight thrust sheets have been sampled for palaeomagnetism in order to establish the amount of rotation, relative to Iblei, which occurred during emplacement. Cfockwise rotations of large magnitude appear to have taken place, and these rotations are considered to be refated to the emplacement of the Calabrian-Peloritani structure onto this continental margin. INTRODUCTION The geological structure of western Sicily is formed by a number of piled thrust sheets. The vergence of these imbricated units is to the south where they rest against the stable Iblean plateau (Fig. 1). The amount of tectonic transportation increases towards the north of the island where the tectonic units occupying the top of the thrust pile are cropping out. The timing of progressive deformation from north to south can be established stra~~aphi- tally because sedimentation was more or less continuous during the Neogene tectonic transport of the thrust sheets. A number of structural-stratigraphic units may be defined (Figs. 2 and 3). These units are geological bodies which display homogeneity in facies and tectonic behaviour, and are derived from pre-existing palaeogeographic units. This paper reports the work of a small joint expedition from the Australian National University and Macquarie University, which, in the 1968-1969 summer season, set out to determine whether bending had occurred and the structural implications of such movements. Palaeomagnetism provides the only method of proving bending. Early magnetic determinations in the Antarctic Peninsula (Blundell, 1962) were interpreted as indicating bending by Hamilton (1966). Further palaeomagnetic confirmation of the Magellanes orocline. In: M.R. Banks and D.H. Green (Editors), Orthodoxy and Creativity at the Frontiers of Earth Sciences (Carey Symposium). Tec- tonophysics, 63 : 97-90. Palaeomagnetic determinations for Jurassic volcanics and a Cretaceous quartz-dolerite sill at three localities around the arcuate Patagonian Cordillera show that a bending of 40” to 27” has occurred. Since the structural bend is 90° it is probable that the Mesozoic arc was originally curved. Cainozoic dykes and sills at Lago San Martin in the northward- trending belt and Sierra Valdivieso in the eastward-trending belt have the same magnetic directions and were intruded after bending. These results essentially confirm the palaeomagnetic determinations of Dalziel et al., (1973a) and further suggest that the collapse of the marginal sea during the Late Cretaceous orogenesis resulted in greater bending in the outer arc than in the inner arc. The orocline must have formed during the Andean orogeny between 80 m.y. and 21 m.y. ago and was accompanied by folding and thrusting. New K-Ar dates for the Dientes de Navarino Sill (105 m.y.), basalt

INTRODUCTION Carey (1958) first proposed that the abrupt curving in the strike of the Cordillera from N-S in Patagonia to E-W in Tierra de1 Fuego may be due to actual bending. This paper reports the work of a small joint expedition from the Australian National University and Macquarie University, which, in the 1968-1969 summer season, set out to determine whether bending had occurred and the structural implications of such movements. Scotia Arc has had a similar and related history (Dalziel and Cortes 1972, Dalziel and Elliot, 1973). Halpem (1973) has dated many of the important rock units in this area. Palaeomagnetism provides the only method of proving bending. Early magnetic determinations in the Antarctic Peninsula (Blundell, 1962) were interpreted as indicating bending by Hamilton (1966). Dalziel et al (1973a), on the basis of Blundell’s and new data, concluded that the hypothesis was unjustified and that the shape of the Antarctandean Cordillera between 68”s and 68” 30’S has not changed significantly since the Late Cretaceous. Dalziel et al., (1973a) also sampled Andean granodiorite plutons in the outer Magellanes Arc and showed that the magnetic directions are deflected around the bend, whereas those for Cainozoic dykes are not. INTRODUCTION Sulawesi consists of two major tectonic units, namely an eastern arc, dominated by thrust tectonics in connection with emplacement of an exten- sive ophiolite sequence, and a western arc, characterized by normal folding, widespread Cenozoic volcanism and granite intrusions. Many hypotheses on the tectonic history of Sulawesi have so far been put forward to account for the complex geological and geophysical features of the island. The most noteworthy are those by Katili (1975, 1978), Audley- Charles et al. (1972) and Audley-Charles (1974). The authors have suggested in these publications that their ideas should be confirmed by paleomagnetic 164 methods before being considered established. As all heatings were done in air, this susceptibility and VRM increase is most probably due to production of new magnetic phases, e.g., magnetite, maghaemite and haematite, resulting from such mineralogical changes as (a) dehydration of hydrated iron oxides (Hedley, 1968; Strangway et al., 1968; Vlasov and Gornushkina, 1973; Collinson, 1974; Ryabushkin, 1976; Elston 271 and Bressler, 1977); (b) oxidation of pyrite (Challis, 1975) which might be a dominant process in the carbonates deposited under reducing environments (Parara Limestone); (c) decomposition of iron silicates (Dunlop, 1972; Larson and Walker, 1975). It is well known (Dunlop, 1972) that newly formed magnetic phases may acquire a magnetization in absence of an ambient magnetic field, because of exchange coupling with the o

case of carbonate samples with a weak initial intensity which are subsequently further reduced during the demagnetization process, formation of such a secondary magnetic component may make it impossible to determine the primary magnetic component. Most red-bed samples showed an increase in susceptibility (Fig. 1.6R) after prolonged heating at temperatures above 500-6OO”C. A notable exception were red-bed samples from the Parachilna Formation and from the top member of the Billy Creek Formation (Fig. 1.6S, Table 1.4), which showed a significant decrease in susceptibility after heating above 400°C. This may be due to inversion of m~haemite to haematite (Turner and Ixer, 1977). The individual behaviour of the specimens during thermal demagnetiza- tion was variable (Fig. 1.5). It was often found that specimens taken from the same sample showed widely different blocking temperature regions for magnetic components of similar direction. This may partly be due to initial presence of an intimate mixture of authigenic magnetic minerals (Larson and Walker, 1975) further enhanced by a large variability in thermomagnetic properties of the transformed phase upon oxidation (Ryabushkin, 1976). Therefore, I prefer to treat the specimen directions as the fundamental unit for calculation of mean directions

e option available, the method tends to be justified as the obtained mean directions could be interpreted in a meaningful way with respect to the mean early Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic data from Gondwanaland and the tectonic and thermo-chemical history of the region studied. The occasional presence of both normal and reversed polarities of the same magnetic component in the same specimen (Fig. 1.7A), points to a fairly long period of acquisition of the characteristic magnetic component spanning at least the period of one polarity reversal. Such a prolonged acquisition of magnetization may be due to the formation of authigenic oxyhydroxides and haematite during diagenesis, and later dehydration and oxidation due to changes in Eh-Ph conditions and/or tectonic and thermo- chemical effects. For instance, Dijksman (1977) observed in Miocene red clay beds from central Spain that the same magnetic direction resided in both magnetite and a haematite magnetic phase. The latter was acquired with a time lag of several 100.000 yrs due to the effect of changing Eh-Ph condition in the CRM formation process. Dual polarity observations were also made in Billy Creek equivalent beds on Kangaroo Island and in some sequences in the Amadeus Basin (Section III). Cambrian-Early Ordovician age is further supported by observations of regional changes in metamorphic grade of especially the late Proterozoic Tapley Hill beds in the Adelaide “Geosyn- cline” by McKirdy et al. (1975). Their observations indicate a general increase in metamorphic grade from west to east across the “Geosyncline”, with most evident metamorphism in the southern part of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and in the northern Flinders Ranges, and a apparent absence of metamorphism in the central Flinders Ranges. Particularly interesting is the magnetic anomaly pattern of the Tapley Hill beds, attributed by them to metamorphic generation of magnetite from haematite (Dunlop, 1972). From a detailed interpretation of the magnetic anomalies (Tucker, 1972), two stages of acquisition of secondary remanent magnetization were identified. Before folding, the beds acquired a remanent magnetic component close to the plane of sedimentary layering in a direc- tion 135” _+1 0. After folding another secondary magnetic component was imposed, again close to the bedding but in a general direction normal to the trace of outcrop. The agreement both in time of acquisition and in direction of McKirdy et al’s (1975) earlier mentioned secondary magnetic component with the characteristic component B is striking.

Three magnetic components have been indentified: (1) A well recognizable recent field component (RFC) of appreciable intensity. This virtually prevented analysis of the data after heating above 450” C despite magnetic shielding. As all heatings were done in air, this susceptibility and VRM increase is most probably due to production of new magnetic phases, e.g., magnetite, maghaemite and haematite, resulting from such mineralogical changes as (a) dehydration of hydrated iron oxides (Hedley, 1968; Strangway et al., 1968; Vlasov and Gornushkina, 1973; Collinson, 1974; Ryabushkin, 1976; Elston 271 and Bressler, 1977); (b) oxidation of pyrite (Challis, 1975) which might be a dominant process in the carbonates deposited under reducing environments (Parara Limestone); (c) decomposition of iron silicates (Dunlop, 1972; Larson and Walker, 1975). (1975). Their observations indicate a general increase in metamorphic grade from west to east across the “Geosyncline”, with most evident metamorphism in the southern part of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and in the northern Flinders Ranges, and a apparent absence of metamorphism in the central Flinders Ranges. Particularly interesting is the magnetic anomaly pattern of the Tapley Hill beds, attributed by them to metamorphic generation of magnetite from haematite (Dunlop, 1972). After folding another secondary magnetic component was imposed, again close to the bedding but in a general direction normal to the trace of outcrop. Samples were taken either as separate sites generally consisting of 6-8 samples or, if conditions permitted, as stratigraphic profiles with each sample taken from a separate bed at regular 1-2 m intervals. Stratigraphic intervals were measured with a Jacob’s Staff and an attached Abney level. Mostly two specimens, 2.5 cm diameter and 2.25 cm height, were sliced from each core. Up to three specimens from each site, or one specimen from each third sample in case of stratigraphic profiles, have been subjected to progressive thermal demagnetization studies. The heatings were done in air in a furnace described by McElhinny et al. (1971). Because of the complexity of magne- tization, all pilot specimens were progressively demagnetized in 12-18 steps with decreasing temperature intervals up to 685°C. The intensity of suscep- tibility was measured after each heating step on a Digico bulk susceptibility unit. The remaining specimens were subjected to partial progressive demag- 258 netization in 8-12 steps over a selected temperature interval. Care was taken to keep the specimens in a very much reduced magnetic environment since the specimens tended to acquire Viscous Remanent Magnetization

components and failure to isolate separate components completely, further AFdemagnetization was not pursued for the bulk of the samples. All magnetic measurements were made on a SCT 2-axis super-conducting rock magnetometer which was interfaced to a Digico mini-computer for immediate data reduction. Directional analysis of all specimen components was made by means of orthogonal projection figures (Zijderveld, 1967, 1975). INTERPRETATION A major problem during thermal analysis of especially the carbonate specimens was excessive increase in susceptibility and in VRM (Fig. 1.6T, U, V,) at temperatures well above 400°C. This virtually prevented analysis of the data after heating above 450” C despite magnetic shielding. As all heatings were done in air, this susceptibility and VRM increase is most probably due to production of new magnetic phases, e.g., magnetite, maghaemite and haematite, resulting from such mineralogical changes as (a) dehydration of hydrated iron oxides (Hedley, 1968; Strangway et al., 1968; Vlasov and Gornushkina, 1973; Collinson, 1974; Ryabushkin, 1976; Elston 271 and Bressler, 1977); (b) oxidation of pyrite (Challis, 1975) which might be a dominant process in the carbonates deposited under reducing environments (Parara Limestone); (c) decomposition of iron silicates (Dunlop, 1972; Larson and Walker, 1975). It is well known (Dunlop, 1972) that newly formed magnetic phases may acquire a magnetization in absence of an ambient magnetic field, because of exchange coupling with the o

Most red-bed samples showed an increase in susceptibility (Fig. 1.6R) after prolonged heating at temperatures above 500-6OO”C. A notable exception were red-bed samples from the Parachilna Formation and from the top member of the Billy Creek Formation (Fig. 1.6S, Table 1.4), which showed a significant decrease in susceptibility after heating above 400°C. This may be due to inversion of m~haemite to haematite (Turner and Ixer, 1977). The individual behaviour of the specimens during thermal demagnetiza- tion was variable (Fig. 1.5). It was often found that specimens taken from the same sample showed widely different blocking temperature regions for magnetic components of similar direction. This may partly be due to initial presence of an intimate mixture of authigenic magnetic minerals (Larson and Walker, 1975) further enhanced by a large variability in thermomagnetic properties of the transformed phase upon oxidation (Ryabushkin, 1976). Therefore, I prefer to treat the specimen directions as the fundamental unit for calculation of mean directions

The occasional presence of both normal and reversed polarities of the same magnetic component in the same specimen (Fig. 1.7A), points to a fairly long period of acquisition of the characteristic magnetic component spanning at least the period of one polarity reversal. Such a prolonged acquisition of magnetization may be due to the formation of authigenic oxyhydroxides and haematite during diagenesis, and later dehydration and oxidation due to changes in Eh-Ph conditions and/or tectonic and thermo- chemical effects. For instance, Dijksman (1977) observed in Miocene red clay beds from central Spain that the same magnetic direction resided in both magnetite and a haematite magnetic phase. The latter was acquired with a time lag of several 100.000 yrs due to the effect of changing Eh-Ph condition in the CRM formation process. Dual polarity observations were also made in Billy Creek equivalent beds on Kangaroo Island and in some sequences in the Amadeus Basin (Section III). Cambrian-Early Ordovician age is further supported by observations of regional changes in metamorphic grade of especially the late Proterozoic Tapley Hill beds in the Adelaide “Geosyn- cline” by McKirdy et al. (1975). Their observations indicate a general increase in metamorphic grade from west to east across the “Geosyncline”, with most evident metamorphism in the southern part of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and in the northern Flinders Ranges, and a apparent absence of metamorphism in the central Flinders Ranges. Particularly interesting is the magnetic anomaly pattern of the Tapley Hill beds, attributed by them to metamorphic generation of magnetite from haematite (Dunlop, 1972). From a detailed interpretation of the magnetic anomalies (Tucker, 1972), two stages of acquisition of secondary remanent magnetization were identified. Before folding, the beds acquired a remanent magnetic component close to the plane of sedimentary layering in a direc- tion 135” _+1 0. After folding another secondary magnetic component was imposed, again close to the bedding but in a general direction normal to the trace of outcrop. The agreement both in time of acquisition and in direction of McKirdy et al’s (1975) earlier mentioned secondary magnetic component with the characteristic component B is striking.

The occasional presence of both normal and reversed polarities of the same magnetic component in the same specimen (Fig. 1.7A), points to a fairly long period of acquisition of the characteristic magnetic component spanning at least the period of one polarity reversal. Such a prolonged acquisition of magnetization may be due to the formation of authigenic oxyhydroxides and haematite during diagenesis, and later dehydration and oxidation due to changes in Eh-Ph conditions and/or tectonic and thermo- chemical effects. For instance, Dijksman (1977) observed in Miocene red clay beds from central Spain that the same magnetic direction resided in both magnetite and a haematite magnetic phase. The latter was acquired with a time lag of several 100.000 yrs due to the effect of changing Eh-Ph condition in the CRM formation process. Cambrian results from the Flinders Ranges, South Australia INTRODUCTION Late Proterozoic and early Phanerozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Gondwanaland continents were reinterpreted recently by McElhinny et al. (19’7413) and McElhinny and Embleton (1976). Using selected pole positions, they showed that a common apparent polar wanderpath (APW) can be drawn when the main Gondwanaland fragments are reunited into the Smith and Hallam (1970) reconstruction. This common APW stretches from the ultimate Late Jurassic breakup backwards to at least 750 m.y. ago, thus implying unity of Gondwanaland during this period. Their proposed APW (south poles) has the shape of double question mark; one half spanning the late Proterozoic and the other half spanning the early Phanerozoic. The overall structure of this APW is certainly acceptable, but detailed examination indicates several discrepancies which make their proposed APW open to improvement and reinterpretation. One of the major uncertainties in constructing APW’s which span periods of appreciable polar movement is the inherent difficulty in assigning poles to either the normal or the reversed polarity group. The occasional presence of both normal and reversed polarities of the same magnetic component in the same specimen (Fig. 1.7A), points to a fairly long period of acquisition of the characteristic magnetic component spanning at least the period of one polarity reversal. Such a prolonged acquisition of magnetization may be due to the formation of authigenic oxyhydroxides and haematite during diagenesis, and later dehydration and oxidation due to changes in Eh-Ph conditions and/or tectonic and thermo- chemical effects. For instance, Dijksman (1977) observed in Miocene red clay beds from central Spain that the same magnetic direction resided in both magnetite and a haematite magnetic phase. Cambrian results from the Flinders Ranges, South Australia INTRODUCTION Late Proterozoic and early Phanerozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Gondwanaland continents were reinterpreted recently by McElhinny et al. (19’7413) and McElhinny and Embleton (1976). Using selected pole positions, they showed that a common apparent polar wanderpath (APW) can be drawn when the main Gondwanaland fragments are reunited into the Smith and Hallam (1970) reconstruction. This common APW stretches from the ultimate Late Jurassic breakup backwards to at least 750 m.y. ago, thus implying unity of Gondwanaland during this period. Their proposed APW (south poles) has the shape of double question mark; one half spanning the late Proterozoic and the other half spanning the early Phanerozoic. The overall structure of this APW is certainly acceptable, but detailed examination indicates several discrepancies which make their proposed APW open to improvement and reinterpretation. Their proposed APW (south poles) has the shape of double question mark; one half spanning the late Proterozoic and the other half spanning the early Phanerozoic. The overall structure of this APW is certainly acceptable, but detailed examination indicates several discrepancies which make their proposed APW open to improvement and reinterpretation. One of the major uncertainties in constructing APW’s which span periods of appreciable polar movement is the inherent difficulty in assigning poles to either the normal or the reversed polarity group. McElhinny et al.% interpretation of polarities presently seems to be the more viable and less complicated approach. However, alternative backwards continuations of the Gondwanaland APW from its well defined late Palaeozoic trajectory, by reversing polarity of early Phanerozoic and latest Proterozoic palaeomagnetic poles (Piper, 1973; Schmidt and Morris, 1977) certainly cannot be ruled out. More palaeomagnetic poles are required in the less densely populated trajec- tories of appreciable polar wandering to solve this polarity ambiguity and for a better definition of the Gondwanaland APW. Cambrian results from the Flinders Ranges, South Australia INTRODUCTION Late Proterozoic and early Phanerozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Gondwanaland continents were reinterpreted recently by McElhinny et al. (19’7413) and McElhinny and Embleton (1976). Using selected pole positions, they showed that a common apparent polar wanderpath (APW) can be drawn when the main Gondwanaland fragments are reunited into the Smith and Hallam (1970) reconstruction. This common APW stretches from the ultimate Late Jurassic breakup backwards to at least 750 m.y. ago, thus implying unity of Gondwanaland during this period. Their proposed APW (south poles) has the shape of double question mark; one half spanning the late Proterozoic and the other half spanning the early Phanerozoic. The overall structure of this APW is certainly acceptable, but detailed examination indicates several discrepancies which make their proposed APW open to improvement and reinterpretation. Their proposed APW (south poles) has the shape of double question mark; one half spanning the late Proterozoic and the other half spanning the early Phanerozoic. The overall structure of this APW is certainly acceptable, but detailed examination indicates several discrepancies which make their proposed APW open to improvement and reinterpretation. One of the major uncertainties in constructing APW’s which span periods of appreciable polar movement is the inherent difficulty in assigning poles to either the normal or the reversed polarity group. INTERPRETATION A major problem during thermal analysis of especially the carbonate specimens was excessive increase in susceptibility and in VRM (Fig. 1.6T, U, V,) at temperatures well above 400°C. This virtually prevented analysis of the data after heating above 450” C despite magnetic shielding. As all heatings were done in air, this susceptibility and VRM increase is most probably due to production of new magnetic phases, e.g., magnetite, maghaemite and haematite, resulting from such mineralogical changes as (a) dehydration of hydrated iron oxides (Hedley, 1968; Strangway et al., 1968; Vlasov and Gornushkina, 1973; Collinson, 1974; Ryabushkin, 1976; Elston 271 and Bressler, 1977); (b) oxidation of pyrite (Challis, 1975) which might be a dominant process in the carbonates deposited under reducing environments (Parara Limestone); (c) decomposition of iron silicates (Dunlop, 1972; Larson and Walker, 1975). It is well known (Dunlop, 1972) that newly formed magnetic phases may acquire a magnetization in absence of an ambient magnetic field, because of exchange coupling with the o

case of carbonate samples with a weak initial intensity which are subsequently further reduced during the demagnetization process, formation of such a secondary magnetic component may make it impossible to determine the primary magnetic component. A notable exception were red-bed samples from the Parachilna Formation and from the top member of the Billy Creek Formation (Fig. 1.6S, Table 1.4), which showed a significant decrease in susceptibility after heating above 400°C. This may be due to inversion of m~haemite to haematite (Turner and Ixer, 1977). The individual behaviour of the specimens during thermal demagnetiza- tion was variable (Fig. 1.5). This may partly be due to initial presence of an intimate mixture of authigenic magnetic minerals (Larson and Walker, 1975) further enhanced by a large variability in thermomagnetic properties of the transformed phase upon oxidation (Ryabushkin, 1976). Cambrian-Early Ordovician age is further supported by observations of regional changes in metamorphic grade of especially the late Proterozoic Tapley Hill beds in the Adelaide “Geosyn- cline” by McKirdy et al. (1975). Their observations indicate a general increase in metamorphic grade from west to east across the “Geosyncline”, with most evident metamorphism in the southern part of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and in the northern Flinders Ranges, and a apparent absence of metamorphism in the central Flinders Ranges. Particularly interesting is the magnetic anomaly pattern of the Tapley Hill beds, attributed by them to metamorphic generation of magnetite from haematite (Dunlop, 1972). From a detailed interpretation of the magnetic anomalies (Tucker, 1972), two stages of acquisition of secondary remanent magnetization were identified. Before folding, the beds acquired a remanent magnetic component close to the plane of sedimentary layering in a direc- tion 135” _+1 0. After folding another secondary magnetic component was imposed, again close to the bedding but in a general direction normal to the trace of outcrop. The agreement both in time of acquisition and in direction of McKirdy et al’s (1975) earlier mentioned secondary magnetic component with the characteristic component B is striking.

INTERPRETATION A major problem during thermal analysis of especially the carbonate specimens was excessive increase in susceptibility and in VRM (Fig. 1.6T, U, V,) at temperatures well above 400°C. This virtually prevented analysis of the data after heating above 450” C despite magnetic shielding. As all heatings were done in air, this susceptibility and VRM increase is most probably due to production of new magnetic phases, e.g., magnetite, maghaemite and haematite, resulting from such mineralogical changes as (a) dehydration of hydrated iron oxides (Hedley, 1968; Strangway et al., 1968; Vlasov and Gornushkina, 1973; Collinson, 1974; Ryabushkin, 1976; Elston 271 and Bressler, 1977); (b) oxidation of pyrite (Challis, 1975) which might be a dominant process in the carbonates deposited under reducing environments (Parara Limestone); (c) decomposition of iron silicates (Dunlop, 1972; Larson and Walker, 1975). It is well known (Dunlop, 1972) that newly formed magnetic phases may acquire a magnetization in absence of an ambient magnetic field, because of exchange coupling with the o

Cambrian-Early Ordovician age is further supported by observations of regional changes in metamorphic grade of especially the late Proterozoic Tapley Hill beds in the Adelaide “Geosyn- cline” by McKirdy et al. (1975). Their observations indicate a general increase in metamorphic grade from west to east across the “Geosyncline”, with most evident metamorphism in the southern part of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and in the northern Flinders Ranges, and a apparent absence of metamorphism in the central Flinders Ranges. Particularly interesting is the magnetic anomaly pattern of the Tapley Hill beds, attributed by them to metamorphic generation of magnetite from haematite (Dunlop, 1972). From a detailed interpretation of the magnetic anomalies (Tucker, 1972), two stages of acquisition of secondary remanent magnetization were identified. Before folding, the beds acquired a remanent magnetic component close to the plane of sedimentary layering in a direc- tion 135” _+1 0. After folding another secondary magnetic component was imposed, again close to the bedding but in a general direction normal to the trace of outcrop. The agreement both in time of acquisition and in direction of McKirdy et al’s (1975) earlier mentioned secondary magnetic component with the characteristic component B is striking.

Samples were taken either as separate sites generally consisting of 6-8 samples or, if conditions permitted, as stratigraphic profiles with each sample taken from a separate bed at regular 1-2 m intervals. Stratigraphic intervals were measured with a Jacob’s Staff and an attached Abney level. Mostly two specimens, 2.5 cm diameter and 2.25 cm height, were sliced from each core. Up to three specimens from each site, or one specimen from each third sample in case of stratigraphic profiles, have been subjected to progressive thermal demagnetization studies. The heatings were done in air in a furnace described by McElhinny et al. (1971). Because of the complexity of magne- tization, all pilot specimens were progressively demagnetized in 12-18 steps with decreasing temperature intervals up to 685°C. The intensity of suscep- tibility was measured after each heating step on a Digico bulk susceptibility unit. The remaining specimens were subjected to partial progressive demag- 258 netization in 8-12 steps over a selected temperature interval. Care was taken to keep the specimens in a very much reduced magnetic environment since the specimens tended to acquire Viscous Remanent Magnetization

All magnetic measurements were made on a SCT 2-axis super-conducting rock magnetometer which was interfaced to a Digico mini-computer for immediate data reduction. Directional analysis of all specimen components was made by means of orthogonal projection figures (Zijderveld, 1967, 1975). INTERPRETATION A major problem during thermal analysis of especially the carbonate specimens was excessive increase in susceptibility and in VRM (Fig. 1.6T, U, V,) at temperatures well above 400°C. This virtually prevented analysis of the data after heating above 450” C despite magnetic shielding. As all heatings were done in air, this susceptibility and VRM increase is most probably due to production of new magnetic phases, e.g., magnetite, maghaemite and haematite, resulting from such mineralogical changes as (a) dehydration of hydrated iron oxides (Hedley, 1968; Strangway et al., 1968; Vlasov and Gornushkina, 1973; Collinson, 1974; Ryabushkin, 1976; Elston 271 and Bressler, 1977); (b) oxidation of pyrite (Challis, 1975) which might be a dominant process in the carbonates deposited under reducing environments (Parara Limestone); (c) decomposition of iron silicates (Dunlop, 1972; Larson and Walker, 1975). It is well known (Dunlop, 1972) that newly formed magnetic phases may acquire a magnetization in absence of an ambient magnetic field, because of exchange coupling with the o

case of carbonate samples with a weak initial intensity which are subsequently further reduced during the demagnetization process, formation of such a secondary magnetic component may make it impossible to determine the primary magnetic component. Most red-bed samples showed an increase in susceptibility (Fig. 1.6R) after prolonged heating at temperatures above 500-6OO”C. A notable exception were red-bed samples from the Parachilna Formation and from the top member of the Billy Creek Formation (Fig. 1.6S, Table 1.4), which showed a significant decrease in susceptibility after heating above 400°C. This may be due to inversion of m~haemite to haematite (Turner and Ixer, 1977). The individual behaviour of the specimens during thermal demagnetiza- tion was variable (Fig. 1.5). It was often found that specimens taken from the same sample showed widely different blocking temperature regions for magnetic components of similar direction. This may partly be due to initial presence of an intimate mixture of authigenic magnetic minerals (Larson and Walker, 1975) further enhanced by a large variability in thermomagnetic properties of the transformed phase upon oxidation (Ryabushkin, 1976). Therefore, I prefer to treat the specimen directions as the fundamental unit for calculation of mean directions

The occasional presence of both normal and reversed polarities of the same magnetic component in the same specimen (Fig. 1.7A), points to a fairly long period of acquisition of the characteristic magnetic component spanning at least the period of one polarity reversal. Such a prolonged acquisition of magnetization may be due to the formation of authigenic oxyhydroxides and haematite during diagenesis, and later dehydration and oxidation due to changes in Eh-Ph conditions and/or tectonic and thermo- chemical effects. For instance, Dijksman (1977) observed in Miocene red clay beds from central Spain that the same magnetic direction resided in both magnetite and a haematite magnetic phase. The latter was acquired with a time lag of several 100.000 yrs due to the effect of changing Eh-Ph condition in the CRM formation process. Dual polarity observations were also made in Billy Creek equivalent beds on Kangaroo Island and in some sequences in the Amadeus Basin (Section III). Their observations indicate a general increase in metamorphic grade from west to east across the “Geosyncline”, with most evident metamorphism in the southern part of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and in the northern Flinders Ranges, and a apparent absence of metamorphism in the central Flinders Ranges. INTERPRETATION A major problem during thermal analysis of especially the carbonate specimens was excessive increase in susceptibility and in VRM (Fig. 1.6T, U, V,) at temperatures well above 400°C. This virtually prevented analysis of the data after heating above 450” C despite magnetic shielding. As all heatings were done in air, this susceptibility and VRM increase is most probably due to production of new magnetic phases, e.g., magnetite, maghaemite and haematite, resulting from such mineralogical changes as (a) dehydration of hydrated iron oxides (Hedley, 1968; Strangway et al., 1968; Vlasov and Gornushkina, 1973; Collinson, 1974; Ryabushkin, 1976; Elston 271 and Bressler, 1977); (b) oxidation of pyrite (Challis, 1975) which might be a dominant process in the carbonates deposited under reducing environments (Parara Limestone); (c) decomposition of iron silicates (Dunlop, 1972; Larson and Walker, 1975). It is well known (Dunlop, 1972) that newly formed magnetic phases may acquire a magnetization in absence of an ambient magnetic field, because of exchange coupling with the o

case of carbonate samples with a weak initial intensity which are subsequently further reduced during the demagnetization process, formation of such a secondary magnetic component may make it impossible to determine the primary magnetic component. Most red-bed samples showed an increase in susceptibility (Fig. 1.6R) after prolonged heating at temperatures above 500-6OO”C. A notable exception were red-bed samples from the Parachilna Formation and from the top member of the Billy Creek Formation (Fig. 1.6S, Table 1.4), which showed a significant decrease in susceptibility after heating above 400°C. This may be due to inversion of m~haemite to haematite (Turner and Ixer, 1977). The individual behaviour of the specimens during thermal demagnetiza- tion was variable (Fig. 1.5). It was often found that specimens taken from the same sample showed widely different blocking temperature regions for magnetic components of similar direction. This may partly be due to initial presence of an intimate mixture of authigenic magnetic minerals (Larson and Walker, 1975) further enhanced by a large variability in thermomagnetic properties of the transformed phase upon oxidation (Ryabushkin, 1976). Therefore, I prefer to treat the specimen directions as the fundamental unit for calculation of mean directions

The occasional presence of both normal and reversed polarities of the same magnetic component in the same specimen (Fig. 1.7A), points to a fairly long period of acquisition of the characteristic magnetic component spanning at least the period of one polarity reversal. Such a prolonged acquisition of magnetization may be due to the formation of authigenic oxyhydroxides and haematite during diagenesis, and later dehydration and oxidation due to changes in Eh-Ph conditions and/or tectonic and thermo- chemical effects. For instance, Dijksman (1977) observed in Miocene red clay beds from central Spain that the same magnetic direction resided in both magnetite and a haematite magnetic phase. The latter was acquired with a time lag of several 100.000 yrs due to the effect of changing Eh-Ph condition in the CRM formation process. Cambrian-Early Ordovician age is further supported by observations of regional changes in metamorphic grade of especially the late Proterozoic Tapley Hill beds in the Adelaide “Geosyn- cline” by McKirdy et al. (1975). Their observations indicate a general increase in metamorphic grade from west to east across the “Geosyncline”, with most evident metamorphism in the southern part of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and in the northern Flinders Ranges, and a apparent absence of metamorphism in the central Flinders Ranges. Particularly interesting is the magnetic anomaly pattern of the Tapley Hill beds, attributed by them to metamorphic generation of magnetite from haematite (Dunlop, 1972). From a detailed interpretation of the magnetic anomalies (Tucker, 1972), two stages of acquisition of secondary remanent magnetization were identified. Before folding, the beds acquired a remanent magnetic component close to the plane of sedimentary layering in a direc- tion 135” _+1 0. After folding another secondary magnetic component was imposed, again close to the bedding but in a general direction normal to the trace of outcrop. The agreement both in time of acquisition and in direction of McKirdy et al’s (1975) earlier mentioned secondary magnetic component with the characteristic component B is striking.

INTERPRETATION A major problem during thermal analysis of especially the carbonate specimens was excessive increase in susceptibility and in VRM (Fig. 1.6T, U, V,) at temperatures well above 400°C. This virtually prevented analysis of the data after heating above 450” C despite magnetic shielding. As all heatings were done in air, this susceptibility and VRM increase is most probably due to production of new magnetic phases, e.g., magnetite, maghaemite and haematite, resulting from such mineralogical changes as (a) dehydration of hydrated iron oxides (Hedley, 1968; Strangway et al., 1968; Vlasov and Gornushkina, 1973; Collinson, 1974; Ryabushkin, 1976; Elston 271 and Bressler, 1977); (b) oxidation of pyrite (Challis, 1975) which might be a dominant process in the carbonates deposited under reducing environments (Parara Limestone); (c) decomposition of iron silicates (Dunlop, 1972; Larson and Walker, 1975). It is well known (Dunlop, 1972) that newly formed magnetic phases may acquire a magnetization in absence of an ambient magnetic field, because of exchange coupling with the o

case of carbonate samples with a weak initial intensity which are subsequently further reduced during the demagnetization process, formation of such a secondary magnetic component may make it impossible to determine the primary magnetic component. Most red-bed samples showed an increase in susceptibility (Fig. 1.6R) after prolonged heating at temperatures above 500-6OO”C. A notable exception were red-bed samples from the Parachilna Formation and from the top member of the Billy Creek Formation (Fig. 1.6S, Table 1.4), which showed a significant decrease in susceptibility after heating above 400°C. This may be due to inversion of m~haemite to haematite (Turner and Ixer, 1977). The individual behaviour of the specimens during thermal demagnetiza- tion was variable (Fig. 1.5). It was often found that specimens taken from the same sample showed widely different blocking temperature regions for magnetic components of similar direction. This may partly be due to initial presence of an intimate mixture of authigenic magnetic minerals (Larson and Walker, 1975) further enhanced by a large variability in thermomagnetic properties of the transformed phase upon oxidation (Ryabushkin, 1976). Therefore, I prefer to treat the specimen directions as the fundamental unit for calculation of mean directions

e option available, the method tends to be justified as the obtained mean directions could be interpreted in a meaningful way with respect to the mean early Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic data from Gondwanaland and the tectonic and thermo-chemical history of the region studied. The occasional presence of both normal and reversed polarities of the same magnetic component in the same specimen (Fig. 1.7A), points to a fairly long period of acquisition of the characteristic magnetic component spanning at least the period of one polarity reversal. Such a prolonged acquisition of magnetization may be due to the formation of authigenic oxyhydroxides and haematite during diagenesis, and later dehydration and oxidation due to changes in Eh-Ph conditions and/or tectonic and thermo- chemical effects. For instance, Dijksman (1977) observed in Miocene red clay beds from central Spain that the same magnetic direction resided in both magnetite and a haematite magnetic phase. The latter was acquired with a time lag of several 100.000 yrs due to the effect of changing Eh-Ph condition in the CRM formation process. Cambrian-Early Ordovician age is further supported by observations of regional changes in metamorphic grade of especially the late Proterozoic Tapley Hill beds in the Adelaide “Geosyn- cline” by McKirdy et al. (1975). Their observations indicate a general increase in metamorphic grade from west to east across the “Geosyncline”, with most evident metamorphism in the southern part of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and in the northern Flinders Ranges, and a apparent absence of metamorphism in the central Flinders Ranges. Particularly interesting is the magnetic anomaly pattern of the Tapley Hill beds, attributed by them to metamorphic generation of magnetite from haematite (Dunlop, 1972). From a detailed interpretation of the magnetic anomalies (Tucker, 1972), two stages of acquisition of secondary remanent magnetization were identified. Before folding, the beds acquired a remanent magnetic component close to the plane of sedimentary layering in a direc- tion 135” _+1 0. Samples were taken either as separate sites generally consisting of 6-8 samples or, if conditions permitted, as stratigraphic profiles with each sample taken from a separate bed at regular 1-2 m intervals. Stratigraphic intervals were measured with a Jacob’s Staff and an attached Abney level. Mostly two specimens, 2.5 cm diameter and 2.25 cm height, were sliced from each core. Cambrian-Early Ordovician age is further supported by observations of regional changes in metamorphic grade of especially the late Proterozoic Tapley Hill beds in the Adelaide “Geosyn- cline” by McKirdy et al. (1975). Their observations indicate a general increase in metamorphic grade from west to east across the “Geosyncline”, with most evident metamorphism in the southern part of the Adelaide “Geosyncline” and in the northern Flinders Ranges, and a apparent absence of metamorphism in the central Flinders Ranges. Particularly interesting is the magnetic anomaly pattern of the Tapley Hill beds, attributed by them to metamorphic generation of magnetite from haematite (Dunlop, 1972). From a detailed interpretation of the magnetic anomalies (Tucker, 1972), two stages of acquisition of secondary remanent magnetization were identified. Before folding, the beds acquired a remanent magnetic component close to the plane of sedimentary layering in a direc- tion 135” _+1 0. After folding another secondary magnetic component was imposed, again close to the bedding but in a general direction normal to the trace of outcrop. The agreement both in time of acquisition and in direction of McKirdy et al’s (1975) earlier mentioned secondary magnetic component with the characteristic component B is striking.

INTERPRETATION A major problem during thermal analysis of especially the carbonate specimens was excessive increase in susceptibility and in VRM (Fig. 1.6T, U, V,) at temperatures well above 400°C. This virtually prevented analysis of the data after heating above 450” C despite magnetic shielding. As all heatings were done in air, this susceptibility and VRM increase is most probably due to production of new magnetic phases, e.g., magnetite, maghaemite and haematite, resulting from such mineralogical changes as (a) dehydration of hydrated iron oxides (Hedley, 1968; Strangway et al., 1968; Vlasov and Gornushkina, 1973; Collinson, 1974; Ryabushkin, 1976; Elston 271 and Bressler, 1977); (b) oxidation of pyrite (Challis, 1975) which might be a dominant process in the carbonates deposited under reducing environments (Parara Limestone); (c) decomposition of iron silicates (Dunlop, 1972; Larson and Walker, 1975). It is well known (Dunlop, 1972) that newly formed magnetic phases may acquire a magnetization in absence of an ambient magnetic field, because of exchange coupling with the o

After application of progressive demonetization either with alternating magnetic fields or with heating, the mean charac- teristic remanence direction is found to be Ilt = 33.3O, I = 4’7.5O (+s = 7.2’). INTRODUCTION The central part of the Alborz Mountains is usually subdivided into seven structural units, viz., from north to south: (1) Caspian Plain; (2) Northern Mesozoic Border Zone; (3) Paleozoic Central Ranges; (4) Central Tertiary Zone; (5,6) Southern Paleozoic-Mesozoic Zone; (7) Southern Frontal Depression (Gansser and Huber, 1962; Stijcklin, 1968). In this orogen the main tectonic phenomena are blocks bounded by faults; the sediments with- in these blocks are often strongly folded, but no large thrusts are encoun- tered. For our paleomagnetic research we have collected oriented samples from the volcanics of Cretaceous age (Fig. 1) both in the Northern Mesozoic Border Zone (unit 2) and in the Southern Paleozoic-Mesozoic Zone (unit 5). Polarities: Apart from the Jurassic limestone sections in which normal and reversed polarities occurred in about equal proportions, normal polarities prevailed both in the Triassic and Cretaceous collections. In fact, none of the Cretaceous samples showed reversed ma~etization and only one or two of them were reversely magnetized from each Triassic locality. The presence of the normal and reversed magnetizations may indicate NRM stability in general and so it is interpreted for Triassic and Jurassic sites. But the Cretaceous formations may all have been deposited during nor- mal polarity intervals including the Cretaceous normal period (Irving and Pullaiah, 1976) and with these just the lack of reversed polarity may be indicative of NRM stability. NRM directions: The tilt-corrected site mean directions are shown in Fig. 5 and we only point out here that they are reasonably precise and all are sig- nificantly different from the present field direction which is also valid for the uncorrected NRM directions. 137 Thus, the stability indicators also support the former conclusion that the thermally cleaned natural remanences are true records of the geomagnetic field at the time of sedimentation. Mesozoic palaeomagnetism of the Transdanubian Cen- tral Mountains and its tectonic implications. Tectonophysics, 72: 129-140. The Mesozoic apparent polar wandering (APW) of the Transdanubian Central Moun- tains, determined from thermally isolated natural remanences at 13 localities, shows a remarkable similarity to the Mesozoic APW of Africa in that they both exhibit the same loop-like movement. Moreover, the difference between the two APW’s can practically be eliminated by a 35’ clockwise rotation of the palaeodeclinations. It is concluded, there- fore, that the region of the Transdanubian Central Mountains was part of the African (-Adriatic) plate up to some time in the Cenozoic when it moved to its present position, resulting in a 35O anticlockwise rotation relative to Africa. In fact, none of the Cretaceous samples showed reversed ma~etization and only one or two of them were reversely magnetized from each Triassic locality. Mesozoic palaeomagnetism of the Transdanubian Cen- tral Mountains and its tectonic implications. Tectonophysics, 72: 129-140. The Mesozoic apparent polar wandering (APW) of the Transdanubian Central Moun- tains, determined from thermally isolated natural remanences at 13 localities, shows a remarkable similarity to the Mesozoic APW of Africa in that they both exhibit the same loop-like movement. Moreover, the difference between the two APW’s can practically be eliminated by a 35’ clockwise rotation of the palaeodeclinations. It is concluded, there- fore, that the region of the Transdanubian Central Mountains was part of the African (-Adriatic) plate up to some time in the Cenozoic when it moved to its present position, resulting in a 35O anticlockwise rotation relative to Africa. Such remagnetization was recorded by Schmidt and Embleton (1976) for similar rock types of Permian and Triassic age from the Perth Basin, Western Australia, and they had to reject a signifi- cant proportion of their samples. A CRM (cf. Table III) was possibly caused by secondary mineralization deposited during recent groundwater circula- tion. No such visual or magnetic evidence of secondary magnetization was apparent in deeper specimens. Partial AF demagnetization to 100 mT in the shallow specimens suggested that at least some remanence is carried by hematite. Results of partial chemical demagnetization do not significantly aid in the interpretation of remanence carriers. Fig. 1). Partial thermal demagnetization and thermomagnetic studies have been carried out on other sedimentary rocks, although the results did not consistently exhibit the extreme changes found here. There are some similarities between the results for the Sydney Basin rocks and those of Dunlop (1972). It is obvious that new minerals with a high susceptibility were formed during heating of the grey and drab silt- stones and sandstones. These results contrast with, for example, those of Shive and Diehl (1977) who reported work on red beds, and pointed out the importance of reduction of hematite to magnetite. It is possible that reduc- tion in the Sydney Basin rocks is caused by trace coal (Permian and Triassic) or detrital graphite (Triassic). Reduction promoted by vacuum pump oils is not a factor in this investigation. Insofar as agreement was found between results from several rock types and differing magnetic techniques, there is good evidence to support the use of palaeomagnetic correlation. Apparent reversals in Triassic samples in this investigation are probably real because Helsley and Steiner (1974) found short-term polarity zones in the Triassic Moenkopi Formation, Colorado. There is a strong indication that near-surface weathering and precipitation of iron oxides has caused remagnetization in the sedimentary rocks down to a depth of as much as 60 m to 65 m.
