ion 300 m thick across the Permian--Triassic boundary has been sampled in the Southern Coalfield of the Sydney Basin, New South Wales. 55 samples, mainly grey to drab sandstones, were collected from 9 diamond drill holes which penetrated the entire Narrabeen Group and the upper part of the conformably underlying Illawarra Coal Mea- sures, as well as a sill emplaced into the coal measures. The samples included fully oriented cores. Additional reconnaissance samples from two further drill holes were also studied. Partial alternating field demagnetization and petrography indicate the magnetic remanence to be a stable DRM. Partial thermal demagnetization above 3OO’C or 4OO’C caused large increases in magnetic susceptibility. Partial chemical demagnetization did not cause significant changes in remanence directions. For the Coal Cliff Sandstone (basal Narrabeen Group, Triassic) the palaeomagnetic pole position (Normal) was calculated to be at 59’N 322’E (dp = 27’, dm = 29’), which agrees with previously published data. For the uppermost coal measures (Permian) the pole position was calculated as 58’N 340’E (dp = OQ’, dm = 10’). Data for samples from the lower to middle coal measures yield a pole position which is between the new Per- mian-Triassic pole position and that for the underl

aven Group, which in turn passed upwardsinto thick freshwater sequences 308 of the Late Permian Illawarra Coal Measures (Wilson, 1969). The coal mea- sures sedimentation is conformable with the overlying Triassic Narrabeen Group of sandstones and shales or claystones with, in the Southern Coalfield (southeastern Sydney Basin), thin cappings of Hawkesbury Sandstone and isolated remnants of Wianamatta Group (shales) (Table I). Exploitation of coal and latite has prompted studies to correlate the Per- mian rocks across the Southern Coalfield, although some problematic aspects of the correlation remain. Facer (1973) showed that magnetic remanence of bore cores presented hope of providing useful time horizons. Further sam- pling and investigation have since been carried out. (Due to instrument cali- bration problems “Normal” should be “Reversed” and vice versa in fig. 2 of Facer (1973)) although the conclusions remain valid .) PREVIOUS PALAEOMAGNETIC STUDIES OF THE SOUTHERN SYDNEY BASIN Reversed magnetization was detected by Mercanton (1926) in Permian (Shoalhaven Group) latite flows from Kiama (about 30 km south of Wollon- gong) and later established by the work of Irving and Green (1958) and Irving and Parry (1963). Irving (1963) found that surface exposures of red clay- s

“chocolate shales”) of the Narrabeen Group carried normal magnetization. The reversed period of magnetization is now often termed the Kiaman Magnetic Interval, although Irving (1971, p. 530) suggested “that the term ‘late Palaeozoic Reversed Interval’ be used”. The palaeomagnetism of igneous rocks intrusive into the Sydney Basin sedimentary rocks has been studied by Boesen et al. (1961) and Schmidt (1976) (Jurassic rocks) and Robertson (1964) (a Permian intrusion). Radio- metric ages for these rocks have been recalculated by Facer and Carr (1979) using new decay constants of Steiger and Jager (1977) (cf. Table IV). How- ever, recent discussion (e.g. Green, 1977) of Mesozoic palaeomagnetic data and the apparent polar wander path (at least partly based on data from Mesozoic rocks of the Sydney Basin) suggests that additional work may be necessary. Agostini (1963) and Henderson (1964) carried out palaeomagnetic studies on igneous rocks in the Wollongong area to complement ground magnetic surveys. Surface samples apparently possessed components of secondary magnetization which could not be effectively removed (Henderson, 1964). Inclinations in bore core samples were variable, even within individual igneous bodies (Agostini, 1963). TECHNIQUES Field measurements and sampling

The directions of characteristic magnetizations are D = 85O, I = -6’, ffgs = 5’ for the uol- canics of southeastern Sardinia and D = 126O, I = -lo for the Nurra samples. The paleomagnetic results display good grouping for each volcanic complex but exhibit a geo- graphical dispersion of the mean directions. This scattering suggests significant motions in Late Hercynian times. INTRODUCTION This paper presents a palaeomagnetic investigation of rocks and ores from the Ktire area, Pontic Ranges, northern Turkey. The studied units comprise basalts (massive flows and pillows), massive sulphide ores, and various dykes consisting of quartz diabase, diabase, peridotite, and amphibolitized diabase. Altogether 113 specimens from 42 localities have been measured. The palaeomagnetic work was carried out at the Palaeomagnetic Laboratory of the Geological Institute, Lund. The object of the present investigation is to compare Permo-Jurassic results from the Ktire area with those from other parts of Turkey, Armenia, Minor Caucasus, Africa, the Arabian Shield, and Europe. It is also of interest to see whether the palaeomagnetic data for the various units can shed light on their relative m

INTRODUCTION This paper presents a palaeomagnetic investigation of rocks and ores from the Ktire area, Pontic Ranges, northern Turkey. The studied units comprise basalts (massive flows and pillows), massive sulphide ores, and various dykes consisting of quartz diabase, diabase, peridotite, and amphibolitized diabase. Altogether 113 specimens from 42 localities have been measured. The palaeomagnetic work was carried out at the Palaeomagnetic Laboratory of the Geological Institute, Lund. The object of the present investigation is to compare Permo-Jurassic results from the Ktire area with those from other parts of Turkey, Armenia, Minor Caucasus, Africa, the Arabian Shield, and Europe. INTRODUCTION This paper presents a palaeomagnetic investigation of rocks and ores from the Ktire area, Pontic Ranges, northern Turkey. The studied units comprise basalts (massive flows and pillows), massive sulphide ores, and various dykes consisting of quartz diabase, diabase, peridotite, and amphibolitized diabase. Altogether 113 specimens from 42 localities have been measured. The palaeomagnetic work was carried out at the Palaeomagnetic Laboratory of the Geological Institute, Lund. The object of the present investigation is to compare Permo-Jurassic results from the Ktire area with those from other parts of Turkey, Armenia, Minor Caucasus, Africa, the Arabian Shield, and Europe. INTRODUCTION This paper presents a palaeomagnetic investigation of rocks and ores from the Ktire area, Pontic Ranges, northern Turkey. The studied units comprise basalts (massive flows and pillows), massive sulphide ores, and various dykes consisting of quartz diabase, diabase, peridotite, and amphibolitized diabase. Altogether 113 specimens from 42 localities have been measured. The palaeomagnetic work was carried out at the Palaeomagnetic Laboratory of the Geological Institute, Lund. The object of the present investigation is to compare Permo-Jurassic results from the Ktire area with those from other parts of Turkey, Armenia, Minor Caucasus, Africa, the Arabian Shield, and Europe. INTRODUCTION This paper presents a palaeomagnetic investigation of rocks and ores from the Ktire area, Pontic Ranges, northern Turkey. The studied units comprise basalts (massive flows and pillows), massive sulphide ores, and various dykes consisting of quartz diabase, diabase, peridotite, and amphibolitized diabase. Altogether 113 specimens from 42 localities have been measured. The palaeomagnetic work was carried out at the Palaeomagnetic Laboratory of the Geological Institute, Lund. The object of the present investigation is to compare Permo-Jurassic results from the Ktire area with those from other parts of Turkey, Armenia, Minor Caucasus, Africa, the Arabian Shield, and Europe. INTRODUCTION This paper presents a palaeomagnetic investigation of rocks and ores from the Ktire area, Pontic Ranges, northern Turkey. The studied units comprise basalts (massive flows and pillows), massive sulphide ores, and various dykes consisting of quartz diabase, diabase, peridotite, and amphibolitized diabase. Altogether 113 specimens from 42 localities have been measured. The palaeomagnetic work was carried out at the Palaeomagnetic Laboratory of the Geological Institute, Lund. The object of the present investigation is to compare Permo-Jurassic results from the Ktire area with those from other parts of Turkey, Armenia, Minor Caucasus, Africa, the Arabian Shield, and Europe. GEOLOGICAL SETTING AND PALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS Vosges In the Moldanubian part of the southern Vosges three sites were sampled 30 km north of Belfort in the Palaeozoic Markstein series. This lithological unit consists mainly of Upper Devonian and Lower Carboniferous greywackes and intercalated shales in marginal to basinal facies (R. Maas, pers. commun., 1981). GEOLOGICAL SETTING AND PALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS Vosges In the Moldanubian part of the southern Vosges three sites were sampled 30 km north of Belfort in the Palaeozoic Markstein series. This lithological unit consists mainly of Upper Devonian and Lower Carboniferous greywackes and intercalated shales in marginal to basinal facies (R. Maas, pers. commun., 1981). The tectonic style of this area is characterized by strike-slip faults and small scale overthrusts of probable Late Devonian to Early Carboniferous age. The characteristic NRM mean directions of the Upper Devonian greywackes yield a mean palaeopole at -24.7’N and 10.7”E. do not possess suitable palaeomagnetic char- acteristics. On the other hand we have found non-metamorphic sediments and volcanics from the Hercynian realm to contain stable magnetization components which may be used successfully for a palaeomagnetic analysis. However. severe remagnetization problems have been encountered when studying the palaeomagne- tism of Palaeozoic rocks in Europe and North America (Creer. 1967; McElhinny and Opdyke, 1973). The NRM of Old Red Sandstone sediments in Scotland has been interpreted (Chamalaun and Creer, 1964) to reflect both partly mixed and partly one component field directions even at the highest thermal demagnetization stages. Overprinting occurred during Permo-Carboniferous times and was ascribed to different formation processes of secondary magnetic oxides (Creer. 1968). Strong secondary magnetizations are also reported for Palaeozoic rocks from the Rhenic Shield (Heller and Kneidl, 1983; J.A. As, pets. commun.. 1981) and the Franconian Forest (Kim and Soffel, 1982). The significant difference in longitude between our Devonian poles and the other European data may be due to an anticlockwise rotation of central Europe with respect to the northern Hercynian Foreland. The Carboniferous rocks yield a mean palaeopole at -41.7’N and 340.4’E. matching the Carboniferous part of the European polar wander path. A fold test within Carboniferous greywackes from the Hat-z mountains proves a pre-folding origin of the NRM of these rocks. However, this stable magnetization direction indicates local or regional tectonic displacement. Our results do not support any major latitudinal motions of continental segments in central Europe during the Hercynian orogeny. The Palaeozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Vosges, Franconian Forest, Harz, Britanny and Central Massif can be used to interpret the Hercynides in terms of a large scale shear belt. GEOLOGICAL SETTING AND PALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS Vosges In the Moldanubian part of the southern Vosges three sites were sampled 30 km north of Belfort in the Palaeozoic Markstein series. This lithological unit consists mainly of Upper Devonian and Lower Carboniferous greywackes and intercalated shales in marginal to basinal facies (R. Maas, pers. commun., 1981). The tectonic style of this area is characterized by strike-slip faults and small scale overthrusts of probable Late Devonian to Early Carboniferous age. The characteristic NRM mean directions of the Upper Devonian greywackes yield a mean palaeopole at -24.7’N and 10.7”E. Some Upper Devonian and Lower Carboniferous diabases are altered (spilitiza- tion), and according to the analysis of their magnetization directions they were remagnetized in the Permian or Tertiary. They require further investigation and are not discussed in this paper. The cleaned mean NRM direction of an unaltered, fresh Devonian diabase gives a virtual geomagnetic pole (VGP) position of - 29.3”N and 18.3’E. Although very weakly magnetized, the Devonian limestones reveal a rea- sonably well-defined characteristic mean direction. The resulting palaeopole position is given by - 19.6”N and 27.4”E (Table I). A fold test within a slightly north-vergent fold could be carried out in Lower Carboniferous greywackes (Fig. 5). The fold test proved to be positive at the 95%probability level (McElhinny, 1964). Thus the characteristic remanence predates the folding which occurred shortly after deposi- tion of the sediments (Alberti and Walliser, 1977). Palaeomagnetic investigations in the Hercynian mountain belt of central Europe. Tectonophysics, 91: 285-299. The palaeomagnetism of sediments and volcanics of Middle Devonian to Early Carboniferous age has been studied in the Hercynian realm of the Vosges, Harz and Franconian Forest (France and Germany). After appropriate cleaning characteristic directions of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) have been determined, which are considered to be of pretectonic origin according to rock magnetic and structural geological evidence. A mean palaeopoie for the Devonian rocks in the areas investigated was determined at -29.7”N and 9.O”E. The site latitude derived from the Devonian rocks agrees very well with that observed in Great Britain and Britanny. The significant difference in longitude between our Devonian poles and the other European data may be due to an anticlockwise rotation of central Europe with respect to the northern Hercynian Foreland. The Carboniferous rocks yield a mean palaeopole at -41.7’N and 340.4’E. matching the Carboniferous part of the European polar wander path. A fold test within Carboniferous greywackes

, 1981). Our sampling has concentrated on nonmetamorphic or very low-grade meta- morphosed Palaeozoic rocks in the Franconian Forest, the Harz mountains and the Vosges (Fig. 1). These areas represent different tectonic domains and different sedimentary basins within the Hercynian framework and are separated by different suture zones as proposed by Burrett (1972) Dewey and Burke (1973) Laurent (1972) and Riding (1974). The sutures zones are more or less identical with the boundaries between the Rhenohercynian, the Saxothuringian and the Moldanubian (Kossmat, 1927) zones of Hercynian central Europe. From the Apparent Polar Wander Path (APWP) of Europe (Irving, 1977) an average pole position of about 160”E, 46’N for the above time interval can be deduced. In northern Slovenia (Yugoslavia, X = lSOE, ‘p = 46’N), 41 sites of Permo-Triassic red sandstones and volcanic rocks have been sampled for a palaeomagnetic study. The rock units are situated either in the Southern Alps or in the transition zone between the Southern Alps and the Dinarides. More than half of the sampled sites revealed that the primary remanence was seriously affected by partial or entire magnetic overprint in connection with the Alpine orogeny. This was manifested by either too steep inclinations, or too weak or inconsistent and unstable remanence. Only fourteen sites revealed the typical flat inclinations of Permo-Triassic rocks. A group of six sites in northwestern Slovenia (west of Ljubljana) gave a remanence direction (N = 6, R = 5.431, D = 151.4’, I = - 11.4’, k = 8.8, ag5 = 19.3’) which is in agree- ment with the mean Permian remanence direction of the Bolzano Rhyolites in the Italian part of the Southern Alps (D = 148”, I = - 20”, after Zijderveld and Van der Voo, 1973), indicating that this zone is still part of the Adriatic plate. However, a group of eight sites in northeastern Slovenia (east of Ljubljana) has a remanence direction (N = 8, R = 6.991, D = 225.9”. I = - 15.0”. k = 6.9, ass = 18.8”) which is more in agreement with the central European Permo-Triassic direction of remanence (D = 204”, I = - 14’). It is therefore concluded that the eastern margin of the Adriatic Plate crosses the region of Ljubljana in an approximately north-south direction. INTRODUCTION Various reconstructions of the Western Mediterranean have been made in the recent years by combining geological and palaeomagnetic evidence (Dewey et al., 1973; Hsti, 1977; Channel1 et al., 1979; Vandenberg, 1979). A common feature was in all cases the assumption of an Adriatic microplate.

section_candidates.excerpt: BONIN ISLANDS The Bonin Islands consist of three groups of islands, each group lying about 50 km apart (Fig. 1). Each group is made up of a few islands and small islets up to some 20 km*. Since the end of the 19th century, the Bonin Islands have been studied by a number of scientists mainly from a petrological and paleontological point of view. Kikuchi (1890) first reported the characteristic pyroxene components in volcanic rocks on Chichi-jima. Peterson (189 1) gave the name “ boninite” to these andesitic rocks rich in bronzite phenocrysts. The rare volcanic rock called “boninite”, a vesicular two pyroxene feldspar-free glassy andesite with a high content of MgO (6612%) (Shiraki and Kuroda, 1977), occurs as the main constituent of the oldest volcanic events in the Bonin Islands. No volcanic rock exactly equivalent to the boninite has yet been found elsewhere (Shiraki and Kuroda, 1977) although similar rocks have been reported recently for the fore-arc region of the Marianas (Hussong et al., 1978). Early in this century paleontological studies of the Nummulites from Haha-jima were carried out by such workers as Yoshiwara (1902), Yabe (1920) and Hanzawa (1925). section_candidates.excerpt: BONIN ISLANDS The Bonin Islands consist of three groups of islands, each group lying about 50 km apart (Fig. 1). Each group is made up of a few islands and small islets up to some 20 km*. Since the end of the 19th century, the Bonin Islands have been studied by a number of scientists mainly from a petrological and paleontological point of view. Kikuchi (1890) first reported the characteristic pyroxene components in volcanic rocks on Chichi-jima. Peterson (189 1) gave the name “ boninite” to these andesitic rocks rich in bronzite phenocrysts. The rare volcanic rock called “boninite”, a vesicular two pyroxene feldspar-free glassy andesite with a high content of MgO (6612%) (Shiraki and Kuroda, 1977), occurs as the main constituent of the oldest volcanic events in the Bonin Islands. No volcanic rock exactly equivalent to the boninite has yet been found elsewhere (Shiraki and Kuroda, 1977) although similar rocks have been reported recently for the fore-arc region of the Marianas (Hussong et al., 1978). Early in this century paleontological studies of the Nummulites from Haha-jima were carried out by such workers as Yoshiwara (1902), Yabe (1920) and Hanzawa (1925). an zone sediments. During the past three years, the entire Early Jurassic to Late Eocene carbonate sequence from the Ionian zone has been sampled at 130 sites providing some 2500 samples. The suitability of these different rock types for palaeomagnetic research has been evaluated as part of a comprehensive palaeomagnetic investigation. This report summarizes the data from white and pink cherty micrites of Early Tertiary age from 51 sites in the Ionian Zone of northwestern Greece. These rock types are equivalent to the Scaglia limestones from Italy which have proved to give reliable palaeomagnetic directions in several investigations (Lowrie and Alvarez, 1975; Channel1 et al., 1978; Lowrie et al., 1982). TECTONIC SETTING OF THE IONIAN ZONE The pronounced similarities between the Jurassic sequences of the Ionian zone and of the Marche-Umbrian region of central Italy were first noted by Renz (1923). The Mesozoic sedimentary rocks from the Ionian zone closely resemble those of the Central Apennines and the Southern Alps and are comparable to the sediments flanking the western margin of the Central Atlantic (Bernoulli, 1967, 1972; Bernoulli and Jenkyns, 1974). The continuity of the South Tethyan carbonate facies from the Southern Apen- nines through the Dinarides and the H

initial identification of lithofacies and age the 1 : 50,000 Geological Maps of Greece were consulted. In the field where recent road cuts exposed fresh outcrops, distinctive lithological characteristics used by Greek geol- ogists served to differentiate between these two formations. In contrast to the uppermost part of the Vigla formation the upper part of the “Microbreccious Limestones” are characterized by chert lenses instead of chert bands, slightly thicker beds, more marly interbeds, and pronounced stylolites and laminations. To remove persistent uncertainty, all samples were routinely dated by micropalaeontological analysis of thin sections and washed samples. CHOICE OF SAMPLING SITES Faulted folds, diapiric structures, and low-angle thrusts, incurred during the Miocene-Pliocene tectonics, result in complex structures which had to be taken into account in the choice of suitable sites. The extensive Quaternary system of normal faults attests to the fact that Greece has long been one of the major active earthquake zones of the world. In addition, the Greek climate is conducive to the weathering of rocks. These factors combine to present the palaeomagnetist with a difficult task when searching for accessible outcrops fulfilling the above require- ments in the Ionian zone

The initial aim was to sample extensive stratigraphic sequences in the different tectonic subunits of the Ionian zone. However, preliminary results of three strati- graphic sections covering the whole Ionian carbonate sequence raised serious doubts about the palaeomagnetic suitability of the Upper Tithonian to Lower Senonian Vigla formation and the lower part of the Upper Senonian to Upper Eocene “Microbreccious Limestones” formation. This was unfortunate since they represent a record of the tectonic history of the Adriatic region during the crucial Upper Cretaceous period. Although comparison of apparent polar wander paths from individual thrust sheets would have been more appropriate, the rock magnetic characteristics constrained the detailed sampling to lithologies which are palaeomagnetically more favorable. Tectonophysics, 98: 1 l-27. On the basis of a pilot study of all the major carbonate lithologies in the Ionian zone of Western Greece., the upper part of the Upper Senonian to Upper Eocene “Microbreccious Limestones” formation was selected as the most suitable facies for a detailed regional palaeomagnetic study. The 51 sites sampled are situated on flanks of anticlines or monoclines which post-date the acquisition of the characteristic remanent magnetization. The regional folding occurred during post-Late Eocene emplacement of nappe sheets which had undergone decollement on Triassic evaporitic horizons. The palaeomagnetic directions after correction for deviations of local fold axis orientation have a regional significance. After this correction the mean palaeodeclination is about 35’E relative to the geographic pole. With respect to the Early T

98 1; Valente et al., 1982). During a study of the neotectonic features of the outer Aegean arc, Laj et al. (1982) collected Neogene samples from some of the Ionian and Aegean arc islands. They found evidence in sediments from Corfu of about 26” clockwise rotation with respect to the present geographic pole since the mid-Miocene. Data from Lower Oligocene to Upper Aquitanian Ionian flysch sections (Kissel et al., 1983) indicate a still earlier phase of some 30” additional clockwise rotation of Ionian zone sediments. During the past three years, the entire Early Jurassic to Late Eocene carbonate sequence from the Ionian zone has been sampled at 130 sites providing some 2500 samples. The suitability of these different rock types for palaeomagnetic research has been evaluated as part of a comprehensive palaeomagnetic investigation. This report summarizes the data from white and pink cherty micrites of Early Tertiary age from 51 sites in the Ionian Zone of northwestern Greece. These rock types are equivalent to the Scaglia limestones from Italy which have proved to give reliable palaeomagnetic directions in several investigations (Lowrie and Alvarez, 1975; Channel1 et al., 1978; Lowrie et al., 1982). ISCUSSION As pointed out before, the Gargano peninsula belongs to the stable Apulian platform which stretches below and all around the Adriatic Sea. In addition it is hardly deformed by the Alpine orogeny and therefore the paleomagnetic results from this stable platform are crucial for a correct interpretation of the geodynamics of the whole area including the Italian peninsula and western Yugoslavia. However, paleomagnetic results from this region recently gave rise to conflicting interpreta- tions. Channel1 (1977) argued that the paleomagnetic results point to a close relationship with the Southern Alps and that the Late Cretaceous paleopoles are not offset to the east relative to Africa by a post-Late Cretaceous counterclockwise rotation. VandenBerg and Wonders (1979) considered that Channel1 (1977) had given too much weight to the paleomagnetic data from Gargano by using site-mean results which had an a95 of more than or equal to 20’ for computation of the overall mean value. ISCUSSION As pointed out before, the Gargano peninsula belongs to the stable Apulian platform which stretches below and all around the Adriatic Sea. In addition it is hardly deformed by the Alpine orogeny and therefore the paleomagnetic results from this stable platform are crucial for a correct interpretation of the geodynamics of the whole area including the Italian peninsula and western Yugoslavia. However, paleomagnetic results from this region recently gave rise to conflicting interpreta- tions. Channel1 (1977) argued that the paleomagnetic results point to a close relationship with the Southern Alps and that the Late Cretaceous paleopoles are not offset to the east relative to Africa by a post-Late Cretaceous counterclockwise rotation. VandenBerg and Wonders (1979) considered that Channel1 (1977) had given too much weight to the paleomagnetic data from Gargano by using site-mean results which had an a95 of more than or equal to 20’ for computation of the overall mean value.
